headline_marked: [[Google's August update]] targets Pixel 10 GPU performance and touchscreen bugs
headline: Google's August update targets Pixel 10 GPU performance and touchscreen bugs
summary: The August 2026 security patch primarily addresses a persistent GPU performance issue and a touchscreen bug on the Pixel 10 series, with a phased rollout for Pixel 8 and newer devices.
details: Google has released its August 2026 security update, primarily focusing on fixes for the Pixel 10 series. This update addresses a persistent GPU performance issue and an annoying touchscreen bug, rolling out to Pixel 8 and newer devices.

The Pixel 10's PowerVR DXT-48-1536 GPU has suffered from performance problems since its launch, partly due to outdated drivers. These drivers were not compatible with Android 16 and lacked Vulkan 1.4 support, contributing significantly to the issue.

Despite several previous updates, including Android 17 in June, Google had not fully resolved the GPU problem. While this August patch is unlikely to fix it entirely, Google's notes indicate it should improve GPU performance under certain conditions.
Beyond performance, the August 2026 update also includes a 'High' severity security fix. It specifically targets an annoying touchscreen bug that caused the Pixel 10's display to act erratically.

The August patch is currently rolling out in phases and may not immediately appear on all eligible devices. It is only available for Pixel 8 and newer phones, excluding the Pixel 6 and 7 series. Users can anticipate Android 17's first Feature Drop, bringing new features, in September.

headline_marked: [[Perplexity overturns Amazon's AI shopping bot injunction]] in appeals court ruling
headline: Perplexity overturns Amazon's AI shopping bot injunction in appeals court ruling
summary: A federal appeals court has overturned Amazon's injunction against Perplexity's AI shopping tool, ruling that Amazon's Computer Fraud and Abuse Act claim lacked merit.
details: A federal appeals court has overturned an injunction that banned Perplexity's AI shopping tool, built into its Comet browser, from accessing Amazon. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals found Amazon's claim of a Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) violation to be unfounded.

The court determined that it was the Comet user, not Perplexity itself, who was accessing Amazon's servers. This distinction was crucial, as Amazon needed to prove Perplexity intentionally accessed a computer without authorization.
The ruling stated that an injunction against conduct not violating the CFAA would not serve the public interest. Furthermore, the potential harm to Amazon did not warrant the initial injunction.

Amazon expressed disagreement with the decision, stating, "We remain confident in our case and are evaluating our next steps." The company had previously sent a cease-and-desist letter in November 2025.

While the injunction is lifted, the core lawsuit between Amazon and Perplexity will continue in San Francisco federal court. Amazon still has avenues to pursue its case, including requesting a rehearing or Supreme Court review.
